core_habit_transfer.note: Do mo_core habits transfer across crime types?

1_background_marginals.criterion: every background value within |z| <= 4.0 of marginals.yaml

2_truth_mi.criterion: summed cross-field MI in serial truth (one crime per offender per type) exceeds all 50 permutation nulls

3_recorded_mi.criterion: recorded MI exceeds all 50 permutation nulls and keeps >= 50% of truth's excess

4_cheat_detector.not_run: state predictability after normalisation: no normaliser exists yet
4_cheat_detector.criterion: row position, case_id hash and FIR serial add < 0.01 AUC over the time gap alone

6_recording_rates.criterion: dropout and crime-type confusion within |z| <= 4.0 of states.yaml; value confusion not above config; structural absence exact

limitations: SYNTHETIC. Evaluating on this corpus measures whether a model can invert this generator, not real-world performance.
Every marginal and loading is an assumption (provenance tag 'assumption'); loadings were drafted by Claude at the project owner's request and need owner review.
Narratives are templated English built from recorded values plus filler sentences. Cross-lingual retrieval cannot be demonstrated, and retrieval on templated text will look easier than on real FIRs.

Background one-offs are generated at style s = 0 exactly (brief decision). Rare, heavily-loaded values are therefore over-represented among serial crimes specifically: a generator artifact a scorer can exploit, and one that moves with serial_case_fraction.
Every case has a ground-truth offender, so non-links here are clean. Real unlabelled pairs are not confirmed non-links (positive-unlabelled); do not carry accuracy-style metrics over.
Validator 4's check that state is not predictable after normalisation was not run: no normaliser exists yet.
Within-crime implications are a small hand-written set (exit follows approach, vehicle class, vehicle_used; gas cutting implies gas cutter). Other real dependencies are absent.

BURGLARY_COMMERCIAL.why: Commercial targets need business hours scouted and more hands to move stock.

VEHICLE_THEFT.why: Quick and quiet; one person can ride away with a vehicle found by chance.

SNATCHING.why: Confrontational street crime of opportunity, usually a rider plus a snatcher.

ATM_TAMPERING.why: Needs equipment and site reconnaissance; skimming is covert.

night.why: Darkness conceals; waiting for night implies some intent.

early_morning.why: Early-morning strikes target routines (walkers, shop opening) that must be observed.

2-3.why: Definition of the group axis; pairing up is arranged in advance.

4+.why: Large crews are conspicuous and rely on speed and force.

crowbar.why: Prying is loud force; carrying one shows intent.

cutter.why: Quieter than prying but still force, and must be brought for the job.

gas_cutter.why: Heavy equipment: procurement, transport and a lookout.

gloves.why: Forensic awareness prepared before the crime.

face_covered.why: Anticipates cameras and witnesses; common when a crew confronts victims.

cctv_disabled.why: You can only disable a camera you knew was there, so this tracks scouting most strongly (planned 1.0). It is concealment rather than force, but a weaker signal of that (stealth 0.5). A solo offender and a crew are equally able to do it (group 0).

insider_info.why: Insider access means a prior arrangement, often with an accomplice.

gold.why: Easy to fence; preferred by offenders with a known outlet.

electronics.why: Bulky; grabbed in ransack-style crimes, easier with extra hands.

documents.why: Usually incidental to grabbing a bag, not a goal.

vehicle.why: Driving a vehicle away from a burglary needs a second person.

two_wheeler.why: Rider plus pillion is the common pairing; bringing a vehicle shows intent.

four_wheeler.why: A car carries a crew and loot; arranging one is planning.

window.why: Side windows are less visible than the front door.

balcony.why: Climbing avoids the entrance but needs a known route.

roof.why: Relative to the other entry points: a roof avoids the street-facing door, where forcing is seen and heard (stealth 1.0). Getting onto a roof usually needs prior knowledge of the building or adjoining roofs (planned 0.5, weaker). Nothing about crew size favours it (group 0).

wall_breach.why: Loud, slow labour that needs a safe time window and several people.

shutter.why: Lifting or cutting a shutter is forceful and easier with two.

forced_open.why: Kicking or prying the door is the crudest option.

grill_cut.why: Needs a cutter brought for the job.

no_force.why: Finding an unsecured entry quietly implies watching the premises.

duplicate_key.why: A key must be copied or obtained in advance.

office.why: Electronics-heavy and empty at predictable hours.

warehouse.why: Bulk goods need transport and a crew.

occupied.why: Entering while occupants sleep demands quiet; often opportunistic.

vacant_extended.why: Knowing a house is empty for days means watching it.

closed_extended.why: Holiday closures are known in advance.

selective.why: Knowing what to take and where it is.

targeted.why: Straight to one location requires prior knowledge.

car.why: Cars need skill and a buyer lined up.

commercial.why: Goods vehicles are stolen to order by organised groups.

duplicate_key.why: The key must be obtained beforehand.

direct_wiring.why: Skill acquired in advance; quick and quiet.

towed_or_lifted.why: Needs a truck and several people.

residential_parking.why: Night access to a known building's parking.

market.why: Crowds cover the theft; targets of chance.

transit_hub.why: Long-stay parking lets thieves time the owner's absence.

none.why: On-foot snatchers are usually lone and opportunistic.

morning_walk.why: Routine walkers are watched and waited for.

riding_pillion.why: Snatching from a moving vehicle is violent and needs a skilled rider.

lanes.why: Escaping through lanes needs route knowledge.

highway.why: Fast exit out of the area, typical of travelling gangs.

defeated.why: Defeating an alarm requires knowing the system beforehand.

4+.en: were a group of four or more

none.en: made no attempt to avoid identification

opportunistic.en: appear to have picked the target by chance

scouted.en: appear to have watched the place beforehand

insider_info.en: appear to have had inside information

wall_breach.en: made a hole in the wall

shutter.en: got in by lifting the shutter

duplicate_key.en: opened it with a duplicate key

occupied.en: struck while the occupants were inside

temporarily_away.en: struck while the occupants were out

vacant_extended.en: struck while the house was locked for days

closed_overnight.en: struck while the premises were closed for the night

closed_extended.en: struck while the premises were closed for a holiday

targeted.en: went straight to where the valuables were kept

duplicate_key.en: started it with a duplicate key

direct_wiring.en: started it by joining the wires

key_left.en: found the key left in the vehicle

market.en: took it from a market area

public_parking.en: took it from a public parking lot

walking.en: targeted a victim who was walking

morning_walk.en: targeted a victim on a morning walk

shopping.en: targeted a victim who was shopping

waiting_for_transport.en: targeted a victim waiting for transport

onsite_branch.en: targeted an ATM at a bank branch

gas_cutting.en: cut the machine open with gas
